heat.anchor_ja: Anchor: the 2021 heat wave (record 46.5 C on 7 July 2021 in the south incl. Turkistan Region) with drought and livestock deaths; values assumed.

scen.10: A week above 40 C: outdoor work shifted to early morning, power demand peaks
scen.50: 10 days above 42 C: water-supply pressure drops, heat illness
scen.100: 2021-type: 46 C peak, two weeks above 42 C, irrigation shortfalls, crop and livestock losses
scen.500: Month-long heat dome with Syr Darya water cuts and fires
scen.1000: Record 48 C with regional power and water failure

heat.method_ja: Loss is an assumed productivity, outage and agricultural cost; affected population is the share exposed to heat-health risk.
assumptions_ja: Loss at k=1 assumed USD 150 M (agriculture-heavy region).
Affected population 40% at k=1.

regions.pop_src: Tashkent city 3,164,030 (1 Oct 2025, Tashkent city statistics office, via Wikipedia) + Tashkent Region 2,975,900 (2021, via Wikipedia); third_party, rounded.
regions.desc_ja: Capital city (about 3.2 M) on the Chirchik river fan at 450 m, with the surrounding Tashkent Region (Chirchik, Angren, Almalyk industrial towns, Charvak reservoir, Kamchik Pass road to the Fergana Valley). Seismically the most exposed capital in Central Asia after the 1966 M5.2 event under the city centre; floods and mudflows are concentrated in the foothill districts and along the Chirchik and Syr Darya.

extreme_cold.note: Assumed from Tashkent climate records (January mean minimum -1.3 C, record low -29.5 C) and the January 2023 cold wave (about -20 C with gas and power failures; search_snippet). Not a ThinkHazard hazard.

regions.hazard_scope_ja: city division (ThinkHazard 39698 Tashkent city; Tashkent Region 3295 values noted in hz_note_ja)
regions.hz_note_ja: ThinkHazard rates Tashkent city High only for earthquake and wildfire (grass/steppe fires) and Low for river and urban flood and landslide, whereas the surrounding Tashkent Region (report 3295) is High for river flood, urban flood, earthquake and landslide: flash floods and mudflows (sel) come down the loess foothills of the Chatkal and Kurama ranges (Bostanliq, Parkent, Akhangaran districts) and along the Chirchik below the Charvak dam. Earthquake High reflects 475-year PGA of about 0.2-0.5 g on the GEM map; Tashkent sits on thick loess that amplifies shaking (1966: adobe housing in the old city collapsed). Extreme heat Medium and water scarcity Medium are the city values; the region depends on Chirchik/Syr Darya flows and Charvak storage. Extreme cold is our own assumption.

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: no large river flood has hit Tashkent city in the modern record; the regional reference events are the May 2020 Sardoba reservoir failure in neighbouring Sirdaryo Region (about 70,000 evacuated, 2,570 houses destroyed) and annual spring mudflows in the Chirchik/Akhangaran foothills. We assume the Tashkent city+region share of national riverine urban flood damage is 20% (Aqueduct national 100-yr 3,037.6 M USD).

scen.10: Spring (Mar-Jun) mudflows and flash floods in Bostanliq, Parkent and Akhangaran foothill districts; local roads and canals damaged, no urban impact
scen.50: High Chirchik flow plus canal overtopping floods low-lying suburbs and dachas below Charvak; Angren valley settlements affected
scen.100: Sardoba-class failure of an irrigation reservoir or Chirchik embankment in the lower region: tens of thousands evacuated, weeks of disruption to the M39/railway corridor
scen.500: Combined snowmelt-rain flood on the Chirchik with Charvak spillway releases; industrial zones in Chirchik town and Tashkent riverside districts inundated
scen.1000: Charvak dam-break class scenario (2 km3 reservoir upstream of the city): catastrophic inundation of the Chirchik valley into eastern Tashkent (assumption, no published study used)

flood.method_ja: loss_max = assumed regional share 20% of the national WRI Aqueduct 100-year riverine urban-damage estimate (3,037.6 M USD, 2010 baseline); k[RP] = Aqueduct national curve divided by its 100-year value (10-yr 0.50, 50-yr 0.86, 500-yr 1.31, 1000-yr 1.47, derived). Affected population, depth and downtime scale with the same k (k^2.5 for population/downtime in the app); not a hydraulic model.
assumptions_ja: Regional share 20% is an assumption based on Tashkent city/region holding roughly a fifth of national urban exposure but lower riverine exposure than the Fergana Valley
k ratios are derived from the Aqueduct national curve, not from a Chirchik basin hydrological model
Sardoba (Sirdaryo Region) is used as the 100-year analogue although it lies outside the region boundary
500- and 1000-year scenarios include dam-related failure modes that Aqueduct does not model

urban_flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: spring thunderstorms flooding underpasses and basements in Tashkent (Chilanzar, Yunusabad, Sergeli); no public loss statistics, all values assumed.

scen.10: Annual: 20-40 cm on main avenues and underpasses for a few hours, metro entrances sandbagged
scen.50: Half-day flooding of central districts, basements and ground-floor shops; tram/bus disruption
scen.100: Day-long citywide flooding with power substation outages in low-lying districts
scen.500: Multi-day flooding combined with Chirchik high water and power loss
scen.1000: Storm-drain system failure across the city

urban_flood.method_ja: No public loss statistics for pluvial flooding exist; loss_max is a rough assumption from downtime of retail, transport and basements in the main city, scaled by k.
assumptions_ja: loss_max 80 M USD assumes about 1 day of lost retail/transport activity in the capital plus basement damage

quake.anchor_ja: Anchor: GEM loss curve for Uzbekistan multiplied by 0.16, the combined share of Tashkent city and Tashkent Region in GEM average annual loss (23.4 of 146.2 M USD). Reference events: 1966 Tashkent M5.2 (city centre destroyed, 78,000-95,000 homes lost), 1959 Gazalkent M6.0 (62 km), 1946 Chatkal M7.5 (about 190 km).

scen.10: M4-5 tremors in the Chatkal/Kurama ranges felt in the city (USGS: 13 M5+ events within 150 km since 1950); no damage
scen.50: 1966-class shallow M5-5.5 under or near the city: cracked panel buildings, collapse of remaining adobe houses, several days of inspections
scen.100: M6 in the Gazalkent-Charvak zone (1959-type) with concern for the Charvak dam; damage to older housing and Chirchik industry
scen.500: M7 on the Chatkal-Kumbel fault system within 60 km: widespread damage to pre-1990 housing stock, loss of utilities for weeks
scen.1000: M7.5 Karzhantau/Tashkent fault scenario at the city margin with loess amplification; losses approach the GEM 1000-year national value times share

quake.method_ja: Loss = GEM national loss curve (10-yr 203.6 M; 50-yr 1.5 B; 100-yr 3.0 B; 500-yr 8.9 B; 1000-yr 12.3 B USD, residential+commercial+industrial buildings) multiplied by the region share 0.16, which is the share of the national average annual loss attributed to Tashkent city (9.6 M) + Tashkent Region (13.8 M) in the GEM loss-by-region chart (sum 23.4 of 146.2 M USD AAL). k only scales affected population and downtime.
assumptions_ja: Share 0.16 is the GEM AAL share; the share of a single large event could be higher because the capital holds a larger part of the building stock than of the AAL
pop_max 0.25 is based on 200,000-300,000 made homeless in 1966 out of 1.1 M residents, applied to todays population at k=1
k values are judgement-based ratios for population/downtime, not from GEM

landslide.anchor_ja: Anchor: Kamchik Pass avalanches (Feb 2023) and mudslides (Jul 2023, 2 deaths; May 2024 road closure) plus spring mudflows in Bostanliq and Parkent; losses assumed.

scen.10: Kamchik Pass closed for 1-2 days by avalanche or mudslide; foothill roads cut
scen.50: Mudflows damage dozens of houses in Bostanliq/Parkent villages and tourist bases near Chimgan
scen.100: Shohimardon-class debris flow in a Chirchik tributary: deaths, bridges and the Chimgan-Charvak resort road destroyed
scen.500: Earthquake-triggered landslides in the Chatkal foothills blocking the Chirchik or Pskem rivers (dam-break risk)
scen.1000: Large loess landslide complex plus landslide-dammed lake outburst

landslide.method_ja: Mudflow/landslide loss at k=1 is an assumed value for a 1998-Shohimardon-class event (about 100 deaths, 100 houses, roads and bridges), scaled by k; exposure is limited to foothill districts so area_max is small.
assumptions_ja: loss_max 40 M USD and pop_max 0.5% are assumptions limited to foothill districts (Bostanliq, Parkent, Akhangaran, Kamchik corridor)

heat.anchor_ja: Anchor: 19 Jul 2026 Tashkent 44.3 C (all-time record 44.6 C on 18 Jul 1997); June 2021 and June 2023 record months; k=1 is a 2026-class week.

scen.10: Several days above 40 C; power demand peaks, rolling outages in suburbs
scen.50: 2021/2023-class: record-hot month, water-supply pressure loss, hospital admissions rise
scen.100: 2026-class: 44 C in the city, 5-7 days above 42 C, grid failures, construction halted
scen.500: 46 C city record with a two-week heat dome; large-scale power rationing
scen.1000: Sustained 45 C+ with concurrent drought and Chirchik low flow

heat.method_ja: Heat loss is an assumed productivity/power-outage cost at k=1 (a 2026-type event: 44 C in the city, several days above 42 C); k is the ratio of peak temperature anomaly to that anchor. Affected population means people exposed to heat-health advisories.
assumptions_ja: loss_max 150 M USD is an assumed productivity and outage cost for the capital region
pop_max 0.6 = share of population under heat-health advisories at k=1

history.name_ja: 1946 Chatkal earthquake (M7.5, Talas-Fergana fault, north of Namangan)
history.scope_ja: Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan border; shaking across Tashkent Region
history.note_ja: Largest Tien Shan earthquake since 1911 (Mw 7.5-7.6, ISC-GEM 7.54, 25 km deep); severe property damage, casualties unknown. Epicentre about 190 km east of Tashkent.

history.name_ja: 1959 Gazalkent earthquake (Mw 6.0, 62 km NE of Tashkent)
history.scope_ja: Bostanliq district, Tashkent Region
history.note_ja: Largest instrumentally recorded event within 150 km of Tashkent in ComCat (ISC-GEM Mw 6.01, 15 km deep), 13 km NNE of Gazalkent near the present Charvak reservoir. Damage not documented in reachable sources.

history.name_ja: 1966 Tashkent earthquake (M5.2 under the city centre)
history.scope_ja: Tashkent city
history.note_ja: Shallow Mw 5.2 at 05:23 local time; over 80% of the city and 78,000-95,000 homes (mostly adobe) destroyed, 200,000-300,000 homeless; official toll 15, estimates up to 200. The rebuilt city has wide boulevards and Soviet panel housing; an Institute of Seismology was created.
history.jp_ja: The Navoi Theatre, built with the labour of Japanese prisoners of war after 1945, was one of the few major buildings left unharmed and is still cited in Japan-Uzbekistan relations.

history.name_ja: Tashkent all-time temperature record (44.6 C)
history.scope_ja: Tashkent city
history.note_ja: Record maximum of the Tashkent observatory since 1881; still the benchmark against which the 2021, 2023 and 2026 heat waves were measured (44.3 C on 19 Jul 2026).

history.name_ja: 2020 Sardoba reservoir dam failure (neighbouring Sirdaryo Region)
history.scope_ja: Sirdaryo Region (Sardoba, Oqoltin, Mirzaobod), 100-150 km SW of Tashkent; Maktaaral (KAZ)
history.note_ja: Earth-fill dam of a 404 M USD reservoir breached after heavy rain: at least 70,000 evacuated from 22 villages (ECHO), 50 injured, 4-6 dead, 2,570 houses destroyed; the Tashkent-Samarkand road/rail corridor runs through the affected district. Criminal cases against nine officials.
history.jp_ja: No Japanese-related impacts found; the event is the regional benchmark for reservoir-failure risk around irrigation storages.

history.name_ja: 2021 Tashkent dust storm (worst since records began in 1871)
history.scope_ja: Tashkent city, Tashkent, Sirdaryo and Jizzakh regions
history.note_ja: Dust 30 times the limit at 21:00 on 4 Nov (up to 50x by one study), visibility 200 m, about 4,000 ambulance calls for breathing problems; Uzhydromet called it unprecedented in 150 years; linked to the 2021 Kazakh heat/drought.
history.jp_ja: Air-quality monitoring (PM2.5) and N95 stock became standard advice for expatriate offices in Tashkent after this event (general practice; unverified).

history.name_ja: January 2023 cold wave and energy crisis (Tashkent about -20 C)
history.scope_ja: Tashkent worst hit; nationwide gas and power shortages
history.note_ja: Gas imports from Turkmenistan halted 12-21 Jan during abnormal cold; a 3 million kWh daily cap, transformer failures and heating loss in apartment blocks; residents protested at energy facilities on 18 Jan and the Tashkent mayor was dismissed on 16 Jan; coldest spell in about 50 years per meteorologists.
history.jp_ja: Offices and residences dependent on central heating lost heat for days; backup heating and power for sites and staff housing is the lesson (unverified for specific Japanese organisations).

history.name_ja: Kamchik Pass mudslide (2 deaths) and February 2023 avalanche closure
history.scope_ja: Kamchik Pass, Tashkent-Fergana highway (Akhangaran district)
history.note_ja: Two women died in a mudslide on the Kamchik Pass road on 9 Jul 2023; an avalanche had blocked the pass on 16 Feb 2023. The pass is the only all-season road between Tashkent and the Fergana Valley.
history.jp_ja: Supply-chain chokepoint: freight between Tashkent and the Fergana Valley (incl. automotive suppliers in Andijan/Asaka) depends on this pass.

regions.pop_src: Fergana Region 4,014,895 (2023) + Andijan Region 3,253,528 (2022) + Namangan Region 2,931,056 (2022), regional statistics via Wikipedia; third_party, rounded.
regions.desc_ja: The Uzbek part of the Fergana Valley holds about 10 M people (over a quarter of the country) in the densest farmland of Central Asia, ringed by the Tien Shan, Alay and Turkestan ranges and reachable from Tashkent only via the Kamchik Pass or through Tajikistan/Kyrgyzstan. It is the national hotspot for earthquake loss (GEM: Andijan 49.6 M USD AAL, a third of the country), for loess landslides and glacier-fed mudflows, and for transboundary river and canal floods on the Syr Darya, Naryn, Sokh and Isfara.

extreme_cold.note: Assumed: the Fergana Valley is slightly milder than Tashkent but gas shortages in January 2023 affected the valley; Namangan foothills see heavy snow and Kamchik Pass avalanches. Not a ThinkHazard hazard.

regions.hazard_scope_ja: ThinkHazard admin-1 level (highest of Fergana 3286, Andijan 3284, Namangan 3291 per hazard)
regions.hz_note_ja: All three provinces are High for river flood, earthquake, landslide and wildfire; urban flood is High in Fergana and Namangan and Medium in Andijan. River flood High reflects the Syr Darya/Naryn and the fan rivers (Sokh, Isfara, Shakhimardan) whose glacier-lake outbursts and mudflows reach towns in July as well as in the spring melt; landslide High is the loess foothill belt of Namangan and the Kyrgyz-border slopes (2021 mudslides). Earthquake High corresponds to 475-year PGA above 0.2 g along the South Fergana and Talas-Fergana faults and the deadliest Uzbek event (Andijan 1902); the Fergana city report (39735) still gives earthquake High with Low flood ratings. Water scarcity Medium: the valley is irrigated from Toktogul and Kairakkum releases controlled upstream.

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: 8 Jul 1998 Shohimardon glacier-lake outburst flood (about 95-104 dead, 100 houses) for the mudflow mode, and the GFDRR country profile naming Fergana the province most at risk of riverine flooding. Regional share of the Aqueduct national 100-year urban damage assumed at 35% (3,037.6 M USD national).

scen.10: Spring mudflows on the Sokh, Isfara and Shakhimardan fans and canal breaches; villages in Fergana and Namangan foothills cut off
scen.50: Naryn/Syr Darya high water plus Kairakkum operations flood lowland districts (Beshariq, Pop, Uchkurgan); 2024-type warnings for all three provinces become real damage
scen.100: 1998-class GLOF/debris flow hitting a town plus valley-wide spring floods; Big Fergana Canal breaches; Fergana-Kokand road closures
scen.500: Multi-river flood with canal network failure and prolonged inundation of Syr Darya floodplain towns
scen.1000: Upstream dam incident (Toktogul or Kairakkum, in Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan) sending a flood wave through the valley (transboundary assumption)

flood.method_ja: loss_max = assumed regional share 35% of the national WRI Aqueduct 100-year riverine urban-damage estimate (3,037.6 M USD, 2010 baseline); k[RP] = Aqueduct national curve divided by its 100-year value (10-yr 0.50, 50-yr 0.86, 500-yr 1.31, 1000-yr 1.47, derived). Affected population, depth and downtime scale with the same k (k^2.5 for population/downtime in the app); not a hydraulic model.
assumptions_ja: Share 35% is an assumption: the valley has about a quarter of the population but the highest riverine exposure in GFDRR/CIMA profiles
Aqueduct is riverine only; the dominant local mode (glacier-lake outburst mudflows) is represented by the 100-year anchor, not modelled
Transboundary dam scenarios at 1000 years are not quantified anywhere; purely a planning assumption
pop_max 6% assumes inundation of Syr Darya floodplain districts and fan towns

quake.anchor_ja: Anchor: GEM loss curve for Uzbekistan multiplied by 0.53, the share of Andijan, Fergana and Namangan in GEM average annual loss (77.5 of 146.2 M USD). Reference events: 1902 Andijan M6.4 (about 4,880 dead, 40,000 homes), 1946 Chatkal M7.5, 2011 Fergana M6.1 (14 dead, 800 houses), 2008 Nura M6.7 (Osh region, 75 dead). USGS counts 99 M5+ events within 150 km of Fergana since 1950.

scen.10: M5 in the Alay/Batken or Chatkal ranges felt strongly; cracked walls in adobe houses
scen.50: 2011-class M6.1 at the valley margin: a dozen deaths, hundreds of houses damaged, hospital and school damage
scen.100: M6.5 under the valley margin (1927 To'rqao'rg'on, 1942 Chust, 1947 Haqqulobod analogues): thousands of houses damaged in one province
scen.500: 1902-class M6.4 directly beneath Andijan or 1946-class M7.5 on the Talas-Fergana fault: widespread collapse of unreinforced masonry, thousands of casualties
scen.1000: M7.5+ on the South Fergana fault system with loess amplification and landslides blocking the Kamchik and mountain roads

quake.method_ja: Loss = GEM national loss curve (10-yr 203.6 M; 50-yr 1.5 B; 100-yr 3.0 B; 500-yr 8.9 B; 1000-yr 12.3 B USD, residential+commercial+industrial buildings) multiplied by the region share 0.53, which is the share of the national average annual loss attributed to Andijan (49.6 M) + Fergana (15.2 M) + Namangan (12.7 M) in the GEM loss-by-region chart (sum 77.5 of 146.2 M USD AAL). k only scales affected population and downtime.
assumptions_ja: Share 0.53 follows the GEM AAL chart; GEM attributes a third of national AAL to Andijan alone because of dense unreinforced masonry housing
pop_max 0.3 at k=1 assumes a 1902-type event in a valley of 10 M people
Downtime 45 days reflects the single-road access (Kamchik Pass) and transboundary utilities

landslide.anchor_ja: Anchor: 1998 Shohimardon GLOF (95-104 dead) and the 13 Jul 2021 Namangan/Aksy mudslides (8 dead in Uzbekistan, 14 total); loess landslides in Namangan and Fergana foothills; losses assumed.

assumptions_ja: loss_max 80 M USD and pop_max 1% are assumptions for foothill and enclave settlements

regions.pop_src: Samarkand Region 4,031,324 (2022) + Bukhara Region 2,107,035 (2026, stat.uz), via Wikipedia; third_party, rounded.
regions.desc_ja: The Zarafshan oasis corridor: Samarkand Region (4.0 M, the most populous province, at 700 m in the Zarafshan valley between the Nurata and Hissar ranges) and Bukhara Region (2.1 M, lower Zarafshan oasis surrounded by the Kyzylkum desert and the Gazli gas field). Tourism and textiles concentrate in the two historic cities; seismic risk is moderate but the Gazli area produced three M7 earthquakes in 1976-1984, and drought/water scarcity is High in Bukhara.

extreme_cold.note: Assumed: Samarkand (700 m) has colder winters than Tashkent and Bukhara has desert winters with record lows below -25 C; January 2023 gas outages hit both. Not a ThinkHazard hazard.

regions.hazard_scope_ja: ThinkHazard admin-1 level (Samarkand 3292; Bukhara 3285 values noted in hz_note_ja)
regions.hz_note_ja: Samarkand Region is High for river flood, urban flood, earthquake, landslide and wildfire (Zarafshan spring floods, flash floods and rockfalls from the Nurata/Hissar foothills as in April 2022, and 475-year PGA of 0.1-0.2 g rising towards the Tajik border); Bukhara Region (report 3285) differs: earthquake Medium, landslide Low, but water scarcity High, reflecting its position at the tail end of the Zarafshan and the Amu Darya-fed Amu-Bukhara canal. Both are Medium for extreme heat although Bukhara regularly exceeds 45 C. Wildfire High denotes steppe/reed fires rather than forest fire. Extreme cold is our own assumption.

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: 20 Apr 2022 flash floods and mudflows in Jizzakh and Samarkand regions (4 dead, 100+ displaced, schools and homes flooded) and Zarafshan spring floods; regional share of the Aqueduct national 100-year urban damage assumed at 15% (3,037.6 M USD national).

scen.50: 2022-class: several deaths, hundreds of houses, schools and kindergartens flooded around Samarkand; Zarafshan embankment overtopping
scen.100: Zarafshan spring flood plus canal breaches inundating Samarkand suburbs and the Kattakurgan-Navoi corridor; Bukhara oasis canals overflow
scen.500: Kattakurgan or Akdarya reservoir incident with prolonged inundation of the Zarafshan lowland
scen.1000: Dam-break class scenario on the Zarafshan reservoirs (assumption)

Affected population, depth and downtime scale with the same k (k^2.5 for population/downtime in the app); not a hydraulic model.

regions.desc_ja: Capital region on the alluvial fans and loess plain of the Chuy valley at 700-900 m, between the Kyrgyz Ala-Too range to the south and the Chu river and Kazakh border to the north. Bishkek (1.36 M) holds the government, Manas airport, the CHP plant and most foreign missions; Chuy Region wraps around it with Tokmok, Kant, Kara-Balta and the Kemin valley. Hazards are driven by the thrust faults under the Ala-Too foothills (1885, 1911 and 1938 M7-8 earthquakes), spring-summer mudflows from the Ala-Archa, Alamedin, Sokuluk and Kemin gorges, winter smog, extreme cold and electricity rationing.

extreme_cold.note: Assumed Medium: Bishkek January mean -2.7 C, mean minimum -7.1 C, record low -34 C; Dec 2012 cold wave (-30 to -35 C in the north) put Bishkek under a state of emergency; winter power rationing (2023-2026 energy emergency) raises the stakes.

national.levels: FL Low; UF High; EQ High; LS High; CY Very low; DG Medium; EH Medium; WF High

regions.hz_note_ja: Earthquake High reflects the Issyk-Ata and Chon-Kemin thrust systems along the foothills (1885 Mw 6.9-7.6 Belovodskoe, 1911 Mw 8.0 Kemin, 1938 Mw 7.0), although GEM assigns Bishkek plus Chuy only about 5% of the national building AAL. Landslide High means debris flows and mudflows from the Ala-Too gorges on to the fans where the southern suburbs are built, and loess slope failures after wet springs; retention dams above Bishkek are the main defence. River flood is Low (Chu, Burana and Kemin snowmelt floods) and urban flood Low in Chuy, but Bishkek's undersized drains and open river channels flood lower districts in cloudbursts; water scarcity is Very low thanks to the Chu basin and Orto-Tokoy reservoir, yet winter energy shortages, Nov-Feb coal smog and cold spells to -34 C are the region's chronic hazards.

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: WRI Aqueduct national riverine urban-damage curve for Kyrgyzstan (2010 baseline: USD 53.1 M at 10 yr to 222.1 M at 1,000 yr) with an assumed 20% share for Bishkek and Chuy. Local events are small: Burana river overflow (Apr 2024), Chu river spring floods, Ala-Archa channel overflow (Dec 2023); ThinkHazard rates Chuy river flood Low.

scen.10: Spring snowmelt floods farmland and village roads along the Chu, Burana and Kemin rivers; a few dozen houses wet
scen.50: Rain-on-snow in May: Chu and foothill rivers overtop, bridges on the Bishkek-Tokmok road closed for days, Kant and Tokmok suburbs 0.5 m under water
scen.100: Several foothill rivers in flood at once; irrigation canals breached, lower Bishkek districts and the Kant-Tokmok lowlands flooded for a week
scen.500: Combined snowmelt, storms and glacier melt; Orto-Tokoy releases plus channel blockages flood the Chu lowlands 1-1.5 m for weeks
scen.1000: Failure or emergency release at a Chu-basin reservoir or a mudflow-dammed river: valley-wide flooding, Kazakh border crossings cut

flood.method_ja: loss = loss_max x k. k is the shape of the Aqueduct national curve (53.1/122.5/144.6/199.2/222.1 M USD) normalized to the 1,000-year value; loss_max = 0.20 x 222.1 = USD 44 M. Affected population, depth and downtime scale with the same k (model convention), not a hydraulic study.
assumptions_ja: Share 20% assumed: the region holds ~32% of the population, but ThinkHazard rates Chuy river flood Low and Bishkek sits on fans above the Chu floodplain.
Aqueduct 2010 exposure understates today's suburban sprawl north of Bishkek; loss_max is therefore conservative.
Depth 1.5 m and 3% of area at k=1 are expert guesses for the Chu lowlands (Kant, Tokmok, Kemin).
500/1,000-year events include reservoir or mudflow-dam failure, which the national curve does not model.

urban_flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: cloudburst flooding of Bishkek underpasses, the Archa-Beshik and other peripheral housing estates (20 Jun 2024) and the Ala-Archa channel overflow (16 Dec 2023). No public loss statistics; all values assumed. ThinkHazard: Chuy Low, Bishkek no data.

scen.10: Annual-scale: 20-40 cm on low streets and underpasses for a few hours, traffic jams, basements of a few buildings wet
scen.50: Half-day flooding of the northern districts and ring roads; Ala-Archa/Alamedin channels overtop at bridges
scen.100: Storm plus channel overflow: 0.5-0.8 m in lower districts and new housing estates, power cuts, one to two days of disruption
scen.500: Multi-day event with drainage failure, mud on roads, retail and logistics halted in the north of the city
scen.1000: Channels blocked by debris from simultaneous gorge mudflows; central districts along the rivers flooded

urban_flood.method_ja: Loss is a rough product of disrupted business days and affected area (about USD 30 M per day of city-wide disruption over two days); not based on a public loss record.
assumptions_ja: Loss at k=1 assumed USD 60 M.
Affected population 3% of the region at k=1 (lower northern districts and peripheral estates).
Bishkek storm drains and the open river channels have not been upgraded for the 2010s housing boom.

quake.anchor_ja: National loss curve: GEM Country Seismic Risk Profile for Kyrgyzstan (buildings, 2025 USD: 25.3 M at 10 yr, 418.8 M at 50 yr, ~800 M at 100 yr, ~2,100 M at 500 yr, ~2,700 M at 1,000 yr). GEM's regional split gives Bishkek city USD 0.96 M/yr and Chuy 0.73 M/yr of the national 31.5 M/yr, i.e. a 5.4% share. Benchmarks: 1885 Belovodskoe M6.9-7.6, 1911 Kemin M8.0, 1938 Kemin-Chu M7.0, 1992 Suusamyr M7.3.

scen.10: M5 within 100-150 km (2026 Chayek M5.0 type): felt by all, people leave buildings, no damage
scen.50: M6-6.5 in the Kyrgyz Ala-Too or Kemin area (1992 Suusamyr aftershock type at 100 km): cracks in pre-1990 brick housing, elevators stopped, Too-Ashuu road closed by rockfalls
scen.100: M7 on the Chon-Kemin fault (1938 type, 80 km): MSK VII in Bishkek, some collapses of unreinforced masonry, days without gas and power
scen.500: M7-7.5 on the Issyk-Ata thrust under the southern foothills (1885 type, <50 km): MSK VIII-IX, widespread collapse of old housing, thousands of casualties, weeks without services
scen.1000: 1911 Kemin-type M8.0 at 80 km or an M7.5+ directly south of the city: much of the old city destroyed, months of recovery

quake.method_ja: loss = GEM national building-loss curve x share (0.054). k is used only for affected population and downtime (k^2.5 convention): the 1,000-year event is taken as 1911-type shaking in the capital.
assumptions_ja: Share 5.4% from GEM's AAL-by-region bars (Bishkek 0.96 + Chuy 0.73 of 31.5 M USD/yr); the 100-, 500- and 1,000-year GEM values are printed only as $0.8B/$2.1B/$2.7B.

An AAL-based share understates a single large event under the capital: for an 1885/1911-type rupture the regional share of national loss would be far above 5%; the 500/1,000-year losses are therefore lower bounds.
Affected population 30% at k=1 (people displaced or without services after an M8-class event).
The Bishkek ThinkHazard division has no data; Chuy and the national report are High.

landslide.anchor_ja: Anchor: debris flows and mudflows from the Ala-Archa, Alamedin, Sokuluk, Issyk-Ata and Kemin gorges after heat waves and storms (July 2024 Ala-Archa readiness regime; April 2024 Burana/Chuy mudflow). scen.10: Small debris flow in one gorge: the Ala-Archa road and dacha plots damaged, a few houses in foothill villages, no deaths
scen.50: Mudflow of 0.5-1 million m3 reaches the upper southern districts of Bishkek or Sokuluk/Kemin villages; dozens of houses destroyed, casualties possible
scen.100: Simultaneous flows in two gorges after a heat wave plus storm; retention dams fill, upper districts and Alamudun villages evacuated
scen.500: Glacial-lake outburst in the Ala-Archa basin plus storm: dam overtopping, mud through the southern city, water supply intakes buried
scen.1000: Catastrophic dam failure with mud reaching the city centre along the river channels; hundreds of deaths

assumptions_ja: Retention dams above Bishkek are assumed to contain flows up to roughly the 100-year event.

No Kyrgyz loss statistics by region were available.

scen.10: 3-5 days above 36 C: power demand peaks, outdoor work limited at midday
scen.50: A week above 38 C with nights above 24 C: heat illness among the elderly, water pressure drops in upper districts
scen.100: 10 days above 40 C: rolling outages, glacier melt triggers mudflow alerts
scen.500: Two weeks above 40 C combined with drought and wildfire smoke
scen.1000: Record 43-44 C heat dome over the Chuy valley with a regional power shortage

assumptions_ja: Loss at k=1 assumed USD 40 M (lost output and outages).

history.name_ja: 1885 Belovodskoe earthquake (Mw 6.9-7.6, MSK X), Chuy valley
history.scope_ja: Chuy valley, 45 km west of Bishkek
history.note_ja: 54 deaths per the Wikipedia list (Mw 7.6; instrumental re-evaluation Mw 6.9); adobe villages of the Chuy valley destroyed. Pre-instrumental.
history.jp_ja: Shows that the thrust front right under the Bishkek-Kara-Balta road is active; design earthquake for low-rise masonry in the western Chuy valley.

history.name_ja: 1911 Kemin (Chon-Kemin) earthquake, Mw 8.0 - 452 dead, Verny (Almaty) destroyed
history.scope_ja: Chon-Kemin valley (Kemin district, Chuy) to Almaty
history.note_ja: 452 dead, 740 injured, >770 buildings destroyed in Verny; 201 km of surface rupture in the Chon-Kemin, Chilik and Chon-Aksu valleys; USGS ISC-GEM Mw 8.02 (iscgem16958130), 80 km east of Bishkek (then Pishpek, a small town).
history.jp_ja: Benchmark 1,000-year scenario for Bishkek: an M8 on the Kemin fault 80 km away would give MSK VIII-IX in the city; expect weeks without utilities and road cuts to Almaty.

history.name_ja: 1938 Kemin-Chu earthquake, Mw 7.0, 22 km ESE of Kemin
history.scope_ja: Kemin district, eastern Chuy Region
history.note_ja: USGS ISC-GEM iscgem902546 Mw 7.03, depth 15 km, 23:50 UTC (ShakeMap M6.8); no casualty figure found (Wikipedia article not available). Second M7 on the Chon-Kemin fault system in 27 years.
history.jp_ja: Repeat M7 events on the same fault within decades argue for treating the 100-year earthquake as M7 within 100 km of Bishkek.

history.name_ja: 1992 Suusamyr earthquake, Mw 7.3, 116 km SW of Bishkek
history.scope_ja: Suusamyr valley / Toluk (Chuy-Jalal-Abad border)
history.note_ja: About 75 deaths (14 by landslides), MMI IX; the largest event within 150 km of Bishkek in ComCat (usp0005cq0, Mwb 7.3, 27 km deep). EM-DAT 1992: 58 deaths, 104,168 affected, damage USD 161 M (national).
history.jp_ja: Felt strongly in Bishkek without major damage; the Bishkek-Osh highway over the Too-Ashuu/Suusamyr passes was cut by rockfalls - plan alternative logistics for the south.

history.name_ja: December 2012 cold wave: lowest temperatures in 76 years, Bishkek state of emergency
history.scope_ja: Northern Kyrgyzstan, Bishkek
history.note_ja: -30 to -35 C in the north, 16 dead, 50 injured (IFRC); state of emergency in Bishkek 18 Dec 2012. In Jan 2012 the city had ~40 power failures a day and 15 homeless died after the CHP boiler failed (snippets). EM-DAT 2012 extreme temperature: 16 deaths.
history.jp_ja: Heating depends on the Bishkek CHP and coal stoves; keep generators, fuel and warm-room plans for staff; expect water-pipe bursts and road closures.

history.name_ja: June 2023 heat wave: 39.5 C in Bishkek (9.6 C above normal); May 2025 monthly records
history.scope_ja: Bishkek and Chuy valley
history.note_ja: Kyrgyzhydromet: 39.5 C on 9 June 2023; 17 May 2025 reached 37.1 C (hottest May day on record) and July 2025 up to 40 C; the absolute Bishkek record is 42.1 C (July 1983, Wikipedia climate table). IFRC heat-wave early action protocol MDRKG016 exists.
history.jp_ja: Air-conditioning load peaks coincide with low hydropower reserves; plan for midday work limits and outage-tolerant cooling for server rooms.

history.name_ja: Energy emergency 2023-2026 (Toktogul reservoir low): winter blackout risk in Bishkek
history.scope_ja: Nationwide; Bishkek is the largest load
history.note_ja: State of emergency in the energy sector 2023-08-01 to 2026-12-31 by presidential decree; Toktogul held 9.1 km3 in Jan 2026 (dead level ~5.5 km3 of 19.5 km3); rolling-blackout warnings for winter 2025-26; regional cuts already in Feb 2022.
history.jp_ja: Offices and plants in Bishkek should assume scheduled outages in Dec-Feb; diesel backup and UPS sizing for heating circulation pumps.

history.name_ja: Ala-Archa river overflow floods Bishkek streets; June 2024 storm floods Archa-Beshik
history.scope_ja: Bishkek (Ala-Archa channel, Archa-Beshik housing area)
history.note_ja: Economist.kg reported the Ala-Archa bursting its banks and flooding streets on 16 Dec 2023 (ice/debris blockage) and the Archa-Beshik housing estate flooded by a downpour on 20 June 2024; typical of the capital's undersized drains.
history.jp_ja: Ground-floor premises along the Ala-Archa and Alamedin channels and the northern (lower) districts flood first; keep stock off the floor.

history.name_ja: 2024 Uqturpan (Wushi) M7.0 earthquake felt in Bishkek; MSK VI in Issyk-Kul
history.scope_ja: Epicentre in Xinjiang, 420 km east of Bishkek
history.note_ja: USGS us7000lsze Mww 7.0; residents of Bishkek and Almaty ran into the streets; MSK VI in Jeti-Oguz district; 3 deaths and USD 527 M damage in China, 67 injured in Kazakhstan, no damage in Kyrgyzstan.
history.jp_ja: Night-time evacuation of high-rise offices and hotels without a plan; a reminder to agree assembly points and check elevator procedures.

history.name_ja: 2024 mudflow season in the Chuy valley: Burana river overflow (April), Ala-Archa gorge mudflow readiness regime (July)
history.scope_ja: Chuy Region (Tokmok/Burana, Kichi-Kemin) and Bishkek (Ala-Archa)
history.note_ja: 24.kg: mudflow in Chuy Region and the Burana river bursting its banks in April 2024, threatening Kichi-Kemin; Bishkek declared a special readiness regime on 17 July 2024 for a possible mudflow in the Ala-Archa gorge and the mayor inspected risk zones. Nationally 25 mudflow deaths in 2024.
history.jp_ja: Mudflow corridors are the Ala-Archa, Alamedin, Sokuluk, Issyk-Ata and Kemin rivers; retention dams above Bishkek are the main defence.

history.name_ja: M5.0 earthquake 69 km east of Chayek (latest M5+ within 150 km of Bishkek)
history.scope_ja: Jumgal district (Naryn), 115 km from Bishkek
history.note_ja: USGS us6000tk5x mb 5.0, 10 km deep; 18 M5+ events within 150 km of Bishkek since 1950 (4 of them M6+), nearest M5.2 18 km SSE of Tokmok in 1972.
history.jp_ja: Felt-but-harmless events happen every 1-2 years; use them to test the staff safety-confirmation drill.

history.name_ja: Bishkek winter smog (PM2.5 up to 30x WHO guideline; top-5 most polluted city in heating season)
history.scope_ja: Bishkek and Chuy valley
history.note_ja: ADB (Nov 2023): winter PM2.5 up to 30 times the WHO guideline; UNDP/UNICEF 2022: households and buildings off the CHP network are the main source, the CHP plant <1%; smog 10-15% lower in winter 2023-24 with gas connections in 31 of 47 suburbs.
history.jp_ja: Nov-Feb health risk for staff and families (masks, purifiers, remote work on red days); the Japanese embassy area in the centre is affected too.

flood.note_ja: Snowmelt and spring rain on the Chu, Burana, Kemin and foothill rivers; glacier melt peaks July

urban_flood.note_ja: Cloudbursts over Bishkek; winter ice blockages of channels (Dec 2023) are an exception

landslide.note_ja: Loess slides in wet springs; gorge mudflows and lake outbursts with heat waves in July-August

heat.note_ja: July is hottest (mean max 32 C, record 42.1 C)

regions.hazard_scope_ja: ThinkHazard admin-1 level: Osh Region (1750) supplies the levels; Jalal-Abad (1748) and Batken (1746) are listed in hazards_alt; Osh city has no separate ThinkHazard division
regions.pop_src: Osh city 454,858 (March 2024) + Osh Region 1,460,425 + Jalal-Abad Region 1,311,007 + Batken Region 570,898 (all 2023-01-01) = 3.80 M - Wikipedia infoboxes citing the National Statistical Committee (third_party)
regions.desc_ja: Southern Kyrgyzstan on the mountainous rim of the Fergana Valley: Osh (second city, 455,000, at 963 m on the Ak-Buura river), the Jalal-Abad lowlands with the Toktogul reservoir on the Naryn, and Batken with the Uzbek and Tajik enclaves. Dense rural population on loess foothills and irrigated fans gives the region 51% of the national population and about 85% of GEM's seismic building loss. Main hazards: Fergana-rim and Alay thrust earthquakes (1902, 1946, 2008, 2015), loess landslides every spring (1994, 2003, 2004, 2017), mudflows and glacial-lake outbursts from the Alay and Fergana ranges (1998, 2024, 2026), summer heat to 44 C and the Mailuu-Suu uranium tailings.

extreme_cold.note: Assumed Medium: Osh and the Fergana lowland have January means near -3 C (Low), but the Alay and Chong-Alay valleys (Sary-Tash, 3,200 m) see -30 C and heavy snow (High); Dec 2012 cold wave left 2 m of snow in Kara-Kulja.

suzak_district.division: Suzak district (Jalal-Abad), code 18608 - earthquake Medium, urban flood Low, landslide High

regions.hz_note_ja: Earthquake High: the Fergana-rim and Alay thrusts produced the 1902 M7.7 Kashgar, 1946 M7.5 Chatkal, 1974 M7.3 Markansu, 2008 M6.6 Nura and 2015 M6.7 Alay events, and GEM puts 85% of the national building AAL here because of dense adobe and masonry housing. Landslide High means the loess foothills of Uzgen, Aksy, Alay and Kadamjai that fail every wet spring (1994: 162 deaths) plus mudflow corridors from the Alay range on to the Osh-Alay and Osh-Jalal-Abad roads. River flood is Very low at admin-1 because the big rivers (Naryn, Kara-Darya) are regulated, but urban flood is High for Osh and Batken: cloudbursts over small catchments flood town streets, canals and small dams (1998 Kugart, 2024, 2026), and glacial-lake outbursts (1998 Shakhimardan) reach the Uzbek enclaves. Water scarcity Medium reflects irrigation disputes in Batken and dry years; extreme heat Medium hides Fergana-valley records of 44 C; Mailuu-Suu's uranium tailings on active slides are a chronic cross-border risk.

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: WRI Aqueduct national riverine urban-damage curve for Kyrgyzstan (2010 baseline: USD 53.1 M at 10 yr to 222.1 M at 1,000 yr) with an assumed 45% share for the south. Benchmarks: 1998 Kugart dam break (1 death, 1,250 houses, 8,760 displaced), 2010 Suzak/Akman mudslides (8,350 affected), 2012 flash floods (9,400 affected), 2024 floods (103,901 affected). ThinkHazard river flood is Very low at admin-1 because exposure is on small rivers and canals, not the Naryn/Kara-Darya floodplain.

scen.10: Spring rain and snowmelt flood village streets and fields along the Ak-Buura, Kurshab, Kugart and Sokh rivers; a few hundred houses wet, roads blocked (2010/2012 type)
scen.50: 2024-type regional event: >100,000 affected across Osh, Jalal-Abad and Batken, states of emergency, canal and small-dam breaches, water supply cut in several towns
scen.100: 1998-type dam break plus valley-wide rain: a district town (Suzak, Uzgen, Kadamjai) flooded 1 m, thousands displaced, bridges on the Osh-Jalal-Abad road lost
scen.500: Kara-Darya/Naryn tributaries and a GLOF coincide; Osh lower town and Kara-Suu border area 1-2 m under water for a week, cross-border trade halted
scen.1000: Failure or emergency release at a Fergana-rim reservoir (Papan on the Ak-Buura above Osh, or Toktogul-type releases on the Naryn): catastrophic flooding of Osh or the lower Naryn towns

flood.method_ja: loss = loss_max x k. k is the Aqueduct national curve (53.1/122.5/144.6/199.2/222.1 M USD) normalized to the 1,000-year value; loss_max = 0.45 x 222.1 = USD 100 M. Affected population, depth and downtime scale with the same k (model convention).
assumptions_ja: Share 45% assumed: the three southern regions hold 51% of the population and most flood/mudflow incidents (Osh Region had the highest regional count, 91, in a recent study), but asset values are lower than in Bishkek.
Aqueduct's 2010 exposure and 'urban damage' definition exclude farmland and canals, which carry most southern losses; loss_max is conservative.
pop_max 5% at k=1 follows Aqueduct's national 1,000-year affected population (~450,000, 6%) scaled to the region.
Dam-break and GLOF cases (1998 Kugart, 1998 Shakhimardan) are folded into the 100-1,000-year scenarios; the national curve does not model them.

scen.50: 2015 Alay-type M6.7: thousands of houses damaged in several districts, hundreds destroyed, few deaths if daytime; 2008 Nura-type at night kills dozens in a village

heat.method_ja: Loss is an assumed productivity, crop and outage cost; affected population is the share exposed to heat-health risk.
assumptions_ja: Loss at k=1 assumed USD 60 M (agriculture-heavy economy).
Affected population 20% (outdoor farm workers, elderly, uncooled housing).

history.name_ja: 1902 Turkestan (Kashgar/Artux) earthquake, Mw 7.7, 5,650-10,000 dead
history.scope_ja: Epicentre 50 km NNE of Kashgar (Xinjiang), 180 km SE of Osh; Alay/Chong-Alay affected
history.note_ja: Thrust earthquake under the Tien Shan near the Kyrgyz border, RFS X; 5,650-10,000 deaths mostly in Xinjiang; USGS ISC-GEM Mw 7.7, 30 km deep. Largest event in the Osh-Kashgar corridor.
history.jp_ja: The Irkeshtam-Kashgar trade route and the Alay valley are in the hanging wall of this fault system; freight via Irkeshtam can be cut for weeks.

history.name_ja: 1946 Chatkal earthquake, Mw 7.5, 34 km north of Kerben (Jalal-Abad)
history.scope_ja: Chatkal range, Aksy district, Jalal-Abad Region
history.note_ja: Mw 7.5-7.6 (USGS iscgem 7.54, 25 km deep), MSK IX, large landslides; casualties unknown (Soviet-era reporting). Largest instrumental event inside Kyrgyzstan after 1911.
history.jp_ja: An M7.5 in the Chatkal/Fergana ranges would isolate Aksy, Ala-Buka and Chatkal districts for weeks (single mountain roads).

history.name_ja: 1994 spring landslides in Osh and Jalal-Abad regions (Kara-Taryk and others)
history.scope_ja: Loess foothills of Uzgen, Aksy and other districts
history.note_ja: EM-DAT 1994 landslide totals: 162 deaths, 45,000 affected, 13,500 homeless, damage USD 36 M; ADRC lists a 14 April 1994 event; an MES official said 90 died at Kara-Taryk alone (IRIN). More than 20 landslides in April 1994 after a wet winter and minor quakes.
history.jp_ja: Loess slopes above villages fail in April-May after wet winters; staff housing and warehouses should avoid slope toes mapped by MES.

history.name_ja: 1998 Kugart river dam break: Suzak district (Jalal-Abad) flooded
history.scope_ja: Suzak and Jalal-Abad city area; Osh Region also hit by rains
history.note_ja: Torrential rain from 18 May raised the Kugart river, which broke a 100 m wide dam: 1 death, ~7,700 displaced (8,760 resettled), 1,170-1,250 houses, 40 offices, 45 km of power lines and 40 km of the Jalal-Abad-Kara-Suu road destroyed, ~10,000 affected (OCHA). EM-DAT 1998 flood damage USD 2.4 M.
history.jp_ja: Irrigation dams and canals are the weak point: a breach can flood a valley town within hours even when rivers are rated Very low.

history.name_ja: 1998 Shakhimardan glacial lake outburst flood (Kadamjai district, Batken / Uzbek enclave)
history.scope_ja: Shakhimardan catchment, Alay range, Batken Region and the Uzbek enclave downstream
history.note_ja: Deadliest GLOF in Central Asia in a century: a thermokarst lake at the Archa-Bashy glacier released >50,000 m3; >100 deaths (93 per Dartmouth Flood Observatory, 14,000 displaced), most in the Uzbek enclave; no cross-border warning. Toll uncertain (25 to >100).
history.jp_ja: Glacier-lake outbursts give minutes of warning; transboundary alerting with Uzbekistan is still weak in the Sokh/Shakhimardan/Isfara valleys.
history.src_name: NHESS; Science of the Total Environment (snippets)

history.name_ja: 2003 Kara-Taryk landslide, Uzgen district (Osh Region)
history.scope_ja: Kara-Taryk village, Uzgen district
history.note_ja: At least 38 killed (17 children, 13 women) when a saturated loess slope buried houses; EM-DAT 2003 landslide: 38 deaths, 211 affected. ReliefWeb GLIDE SL-2003-000177-KGZ.
history.jp_ja: Villages had been warned and partly relocated; the recurrence at the same site (1994, 2003) shows slope monitoring must be followed by enforced relocation.

history.name_ja: 2004 Budalyk landslide, Alay district (Osh Region)
history.scope_ja: Budalyk village, Alay district
history.note_ja: 33 killed (16 children), 11 injured; government appealed for international aid. EM-DAT 2004 landslide totals: 49 deaths (annual). ReliefWeb GLIDE LS-2003-000177-KGZ.
history.jp_ja: Alay valley villages along the Osh-Irkeshtam road (M41/A371) are exposed; road cuts stop China-bound trucks for days.

history.name_ja: 2008 Nura earthquake, Mw 6.6-6.7, Alay district (Osh Region)
history.scope_ja: Nura village near Irkeshtam, Alay district
history.note_ja: Nura destroyed; 75 dead and 150 injured (Wikipedia), EM-DAT 74 deaths and 4,197 affected, GEM 74; USGS usp000gjd4 Mwc 6.7, 27 km deep; 131 km SE of Nookat. ReliefWeb EQ-2008-000181-KGZ.
history.jp_ja: Adobe housing collapsed at night; the same building stock dominates Osh Region villages, so casualties scale with population density, not magnitude.

history.name_ja: 2015 Osh Region earthquake, Mw 6.7 (Alay district): 6 districts damaged, no deaths
history.scope_ja: Kara-Suu, Alay, Ozgon, Kara-Kulja, Aravan, Chong-Alay districts
history.note_ja: IFRC: >15,000 people (3,300 families) affected, >200 houses destroyed and >800 severely damaged (ACTED later counted 6,576 damaged houses), schools, mosques and health posts hit; no casualties. EM-DAT 2015 earthquake: 16,780 affected, damage USD 12 M. ReliefWeb EQ-2015-000158-KGZ.
history.jp_ja: A no-fatality M6.7 shows the benefit of daytime timing and low-rise housing; damage to schools and clinics still took a year of 'build back safer' work.

history.name_ja: 2017 Ayu landslide, Uzgen district (Osh Region): 24 dead
history.scope_ja: Ayu village, Uzgen district
history.note_ja: A landslide buried 6-7 houses at dawn, killing all 24 occupants incl. 9 children; 266 rescuers; 40 families evacuated; the village had been evacuated in March for slope instability but people returned. EM-DAT 2017 landslide: 24 deaths. National mourning 30 April.
history.jp_ja: Evacuation orders are lifted or ignored when slopes look stable; companies should keep their own exclusion rules for staff living below monitored slopes.

history.name_ja: 2024 floods and mudflows: Osh city, Osh, Jalal-Abad, Batken, Talas, Naryn (states of emergency)
history.scope_ja: Osh city and 23 villages of Osh Region, 6 villages in Jalal-Abad, Razzakov (Batken); June mudflows in Jalal-Abad, Osh and Batken
history.note_ja: 20-24 April 2024 rain (more than a normal April in 8 days): 103,901 affected, 1 death, hundreds evacuated in Osh Region, 300 families in Jalal-Abad; emergencies in Osh, Jalal-Abad, Talas. 17-24 June mudflows hit >500 families, killed a 5-year-old in Batken, cut water in Kadamjai; DREF MDRKG019 CHF 488,376. 25 mudflow deaths nationally in 2024.
history.jp_ja: Mudflows blocked the Osh-Bishkek and Myrza-Ake-Kara-Shoro roads and cut drinking water; Osh city streets flooded - supply-chain and site access plans need the April-July window.

history.name_ja: 2026 mudflow season: Osh-Alay highway mudflow kills 6; Nooken (Jalal-Abad) mudflows flood Kochkor-Ata (13 July)
history.scope_ja: Osh-Alay highway (Osh Region); Nooken district, Jalal-Abad Region
history.note_ja: A 24 June 2026 mudflow swept a car off the Osh-Alay highway killing six - the deadliest of at least eight mudflow deaths in 2026 (snippet); on 13 July 2026 short intense rain over Nooken sent mudflows down the Besh-Korgon and Kara-Bulak channels into Kochkor-Ata and four villages, state of emergency in the district (IFRC). ReliefWeb FL-2026-000114-KGZ.
history.jp_ja: Evening cloudbursts over small catchments give under an hour of warning; drivers on the Alay and Fergana-rim roads are the most exposed group.

flood.note_ja: Spring rain plus snowmelt (April-June); glacier-fed peaks and GLOFs in July

urban_flood.note_ja: Cloudbursts over the Fergana rim flood town streets and channels

landslide.note_ja: Loess slides peak April-May after wet winters; mudflows continue into July

cold.note_ja: Mild in Osh, severe in the Alay valley (Sary-Tash)

water.note_ja: Late-summer irrigation shortage in Batken and dry years

regions.name_ja: Dushanbe and Districts of Republican Subordination
regions.name_en: Dushanbe and Districts of Republican Subordination
regions.pop_src: Dushanbe city 1,228,400 (March 2024) + Districts of Republican Subordination 2,165,900 (2020), both Wikipedia infoboxes (third_party), rounded; 3.4-3.5 M is the working figure.
regions.desc_ja: The capital (1.2 M, 820 m) sits in the Hisor valley on the Varzob and Kofarnihon rivers between the Hisor range and the loess hills of Rudaki; the surrounding Districts of Republican Subordination (DRS, 2.2 M) run east through Vahdat and the Nurek/Roghun dams to the Rasht (Surkhob) valley and the Kyrgyz border. It is the national hub for government, the Dushanbe-Khujand (Anzob) and Dushanbe-Khorog roads, the airport and the Tursunzoda aluminium smelter. Key hazards: earthquakes (1907 Karatag, 1949 Khait, 1989 Hisor), spring mudflows and flash floods in every side valley, and winter energy shocks.

extreme_cold.note: Dushanbe January mean 3.1 C, record low -26.6 C: temperatures are moderate, but the 2008 cold wave (below -20 C, no heating, power rationing) showed high systemic vulnerability; mountain districts of the DRS (Rasht, Lakhsh) are colder and snowbound.

regions.hazard_scope_ja: ThinkHazard admin-1 level (2850 'Tadzhikistan Territories' = DRS incl. Dushanbe city; district reports Rudaki 37623 and Varzob 37630 noted)
regions.hz_note_ja: ThinkHazard 2850 rates urban flood, earthquake, landslide and wildfire High, river flood only Low (DRS rivers are steep torrents), extreme heat and water scarcity Medium; the Rudaki (37623) and Varzob (37630) district reports both give landslide High. Locally the dominant hazards are mudflow corridors on every tributary of the Varzob, Luchob, Kofarnihon and Surkhob (Aug 2023: 21 deaths; Varzob mudslides cut the city's water in 1993, 2004 and 2016), loess soils that flow when shaken (Sharora 1989, Khait 1949), and intensity-IX seismic zoning for most of the city with the Hissar-Kokshaal fault 10-15 km north and the Ilyak-Vakhsh fault 20-25 km south. Extreme cold is our own assumption: winters are mild (January mean 3.1 C) but the 2008 energy crisis left the capital without heating for weeks.

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: WRI Aqueduct national riverine urban-damage curve for Tajikistan (100-yr USD 138.6 M, 1000-yr 202.2 M, 2010 baseline) with an assumed Dushanbe+DRS share of 30%. Reference events: 1993 Varzob flood (about 1,000 m3/s; bridges, Dushanbe-Khujand road and water intakes destroyed), July 2004 floods (400,000 in the capital without clean water), April 1998 Navdi/Gharm floods and landslides (50 dead), spring 2010 floods in 21 districts (EM-DAT: 75 deaths, USD 204 M nationally).

scen.10: Spring (Apr-Jun) high water on the Varzob, Luchob and Kofarnihon: riverside dachas, roads and water intakes in Varzob gorge damaged, 1-2 days of turbid or interrupted city water
scen.50: 2004/2016-type: Varzob mudflow-flood blocks the intake, downtown Dushanbe without water for 1-3 days, bridges on the Khujand road lost, hundreds of houses in Rudaki/Hisor flooded
scen.100: 1993-class Varzob flood (about 1,000 m3/s) plus Kofarnihon and Surkhob floods in Vahdat and Rasht: thousands of houses, irrigation and power lines damaged
scen.500: Basin-wide rain-on-snow flood with failure of mudflow-protection dykes; low-lying Dushanbe districts inundated for days
scen.1000: Cascading event: extreme basin-wide flood with a dam-safety incident on the Vakhsh (Nurek/Roghun) or Kofarnihon reservoirs (assumption)

flood.method_ja: loss_max = 30% (assumed share) of the Aqueduct national 1000-year riverine urban damage (USD 202.2 M); k[RP] = Aqueduct national curve / its 1000-year value (derived). Depth, area and population scale with k (k^2.5 for population and downtime in the app); not a hydraulic model.
assumptions_ja: 30% share is an assumption: Dushanbe+DRS hold about a third of the population, but Khatlon has the largest floodplains (assumed 40%), Sughd 25%, GBAO 5%
pop_max 0.05 = Aqueduct 1000-yr affected population (571,600 nationally) x 30% / 3.4 M
Aqueduct is riverine only and ignores the mudflow mechanism behind most local damage (see landslide row)
500/1000-yr scenarios add dam-related failure modes that Aqueduct does not model

urban_flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: short convective downpours and hail flood Dushanbe streets every spring; the late-August 2023 storm is the recent reference. No public loss statistics exist, so all values are assumptions.

scen.10: Annual: 20-40 cm of water on Rudaki Avenue underpasses and in the Sino/Shohmansur low spots for a few hours, traffic jams, basement shops wet
scen.50: Half a day of city-wide ponding, drainage canals overflow, power cuts in several districts, Varzob road closed by small mudflows
scen.100: 2023-type multi-day rain: mudflows from the Luchob/Varzob slopes into northern districts, 1-2 days of disruption, deaths in peri-urban Rudaki/Vahdat
scen.500: Several days of flooding plus loss of water and power across the city
scen.1000: Failure of the storm drainage and water system for a week

urban_flood.method_ja: Loss assumed from disruption days (about USD 10-15 M per day of lost activity in the capital), not from statistics.
assumptions_ja: Dushanbe generates roughly a third of national GDP (assumption)
Depth and area refer to the built-up part of the city, not the DRS

quake.anchor_ja: Anchor: GEM national building-loss curve for Tajikistan (10-yr USD 29.1 M, 50-yr 268.7 M, 100-yr 478.1 M, 500-yr about 1.4 B, 1000-yr about 2.5 B) x 0.44, the share of national average annual loss attributed to Dushanbe city (USD 4.6 M) and the DRS (6.5 M) in GEM's loss-by-region chart (11.1 of 25.27 M). Reference events: 1907 Karatag M7.4 (100 km W, 12,000+ dead), 1930 Dushanbe M6.3 (175 dead), 1949 Khait M7.5 (about 7,200 dead), 1989 Hisor mb 5.3 (13 km W, 274 dead), 2025 Rasht Mw 5.8.

scen.10: M4.5-5.5 shocks in the Rasht valley or Hisor range felt at intensity 3-5 in the city (USGS: 50 M5+ within 150 km since 1950); cracked plaster, no structural damage
scen.50: 2025 Rasht / 1989 Hisor type: M5.5-5.8 within 50-150 km; hundreds of rural houses destroyed, loess flowslides bury villages, a few deaths
scen.100: 1930-type M6-6.5 under the Hisor valley: collapse of adobe and unreinforced masonry in old districts, panel blocks damaged, thousands homeless
scen.500: 1907 Karatag-type M7.4 within 60-100 km on the Hisor range: widespread damage in Tursunzoda, Hisor, Shahrinav and western Dushanbe; weeks without utilities
scen.1000: M7.5 on the Ilyak-Vakhsh or Hissar-Kokshaal faults near the city with intensity IX and soft-soil amplification; loss about USD 1.1 B (GEM 1000-yr x share)

quake.method_ja: Loss = GEM national loss curve x region share 0.44 (derived from GEM's regional AAL split). k only scales affected population and downtime (k^2.5 in the app). GEM counts buildings only; lifelines and indirect losses are excluded.
assumptions_ja: Share 0.44 is the AAL share; a near-field event under the capital could carry a larger share because Dushanbe holds a disproportionate part of the building stock
pop_max 0.3 reflects GEM's building stock (adobe and unreinforced masonry dominate by count) and the 1949/1907 experience
k values are judgement-based ratios for population and downtime, not from GEM

landslide.anchor_ja: Anchor: mudflows, debris flows and loess landslides are the most frequent killers in the DRS (CoES: about 40% of incidents). References: 1949 Khait flowslides (about 7,200 dead), 1989 Sharora (274 dead), April 1998 Navdi/Gharm (50 dead), Aug 2023 Vahdat-Rudaki-Varzob (21 dead), May 2024 Varzob (1 dead), Feb 2023 Varzob avalanche (1 dead). Loss values are assumptions (2025 Rasht quake damage USD 1.66 M; 2010 national flood/mudflow year USD 204 M).

scen.10: Normal season: dozens of mudflows in Varzob, Rudaki, Vahdat, Hisor and Rasht; a few houses and roads lost, 1-5 deaths
scen.50: 2023-type: multi-day rain, 20+ deaths, hundreds of houses, Dushanbe-Vahdat-Lakhsh highway cut
scen.100: 1998-type valley-wide landslides in the Rasht/Surkhob valley or a Varzob debris flow reaching the northern suburbs
scen.500: 1989-type earthquake-triggered loess flowslides burying villages at the Hisor valley margin
scen.1000: 1949 Khait-type rock avalanche and valley-length flowslides after an M7+ in the Rasht valley

landslide.method_ja: Loss, area and population are expert assumptions scaled by k; k[1000]=1 corresponds to a 1949-type cascade. Use together with the quake row (shared trigger).
assumptions_ja: loss_max USD 40 M at k=1 is an order-of-magnitude assumption for a 1949-type event hitting today's Rasht/Hisor settlements
pop_max 0.02 (about 70,000 people affected) assumes dozens of villages in the Rasht valley and Hisor foothills
Snow avalanches on the Anzob and Khorog roads are counted here as mass movement

heat.anchor_ja: Anchor: Dushanbe record 45.0 C, July mean maximum 36.4 C; Tajikhydromet warned of +44 to +47 C in July 2018 and July 2025 together with dust storms. Heat coincides with peak electricity demand.

scen.10: A week above 40 C: outdoor work limited to mornings, water pressure drops, dust haze
scen.50: Two weeks of 42-45 C with power cuts; heat casualties among outdoor workers and the elderly
scen.100: Record 46 C spell with glacier-melt mudflows (2015-type) in the mountains
scen.500: Three-week heat dome with grid failure and water shortage
scen.1000: Season-long extreme heat with crop failure in the Hisor valley

heat.method_ja: Assumed losses from productivity and power-system stress; no official heat statistics found.
assumptions_ja: pop_max 0.3 = share of residents exposed outdoors or without cooling at k=1
loss_max USD 20 M is an assumption (about 1-2 days of capital-region output)

history.name_ja: 1907 Karatag (Qaratog) earthquake, Ms 7.4 / Mw 7.44, Hisor range
history.scope_ja: Tajikistan-Uzbekistan border, 100 km W of Dushanbe
history.note_ja: 12,000-15,000 dead (Wikipedia; GEM 12,000); largest catalogued event within 150 km of Dushanbe (USGS iscgem16957975); destroyed Qaratog and villages of today's Tursunzoda/Shahrinav districts.
history.jp_ja: Worst-case shaking scenario for sites in western Dushanbe, Hisor and Tursunzoda.

history.name_ja: 1930 Dushanbe earthquake, M6.3
history.scope_ja: Dushanbe (then Stalinabad) and Hisor valley
history.note_ja: 175 deaths per Wikipedia's earthquake list and EM-DAT 1930; absent from the USGS ISC-GEM M6+ list, so magnitude/location rest on the Wikipedia table. The only damaging shock recorded directly under the capital.

history.name_ja: 1949 Khait (Hoit) earthquake, Mw 7.5, and Khait landslide, Rasht valley
history.scope_ja: Rasht (Gharm) valley, DRS, 190 km E of Dushanbe
history.note_ja: About 7,200 dead (range 5,000-28,000; GEM 3,500), mostly in loess flowslides; Khait and Khisorak buried, 33 villages destroyed. USGS iscgem896645.
history.jp_ja: Template for quake-triggered landslide risk on the Dushanbe-Rasht-Lakhsh corridor.

history.name_ja: 1989 Hisor (Gissar) earthquake, mb 5.3, Sharora loess flowslides
history.scope_ja: Sharora, Hisor district, 13 km W of Dushanbe
history.note_ja: Nearly all 274 deaths from loess flows that buried Sharora and two villages; MMI VII; damage USD 24 M; USGS usp0003r4d, the nearest M5+ to Dushanbe since 1950 (13.5 km).
history.jp_ja: Shows that even an M5 can be deadly on the loess terraces west of the city.

history.name_ja: April 1998 floods and landslides: Navdi (Rasht), Ayni, Shahrinav, Varzob, Kulob
history.scope_ja: Rasht valley worst hit; also Varzob/Shahrinav near Dushanbe and Kulob
history.note_ja: Rain from 23 April; Navdi landslide 50 dead, 12 missing, 60 houses destroyed; Kulob 2,000 affected. EM-DAT 1998: 51 flood + 11 landslide deaths, USD 66 M.

history.name_ja: July 2004 floods and landslides: Dushanbe water supply cut, Varzob road destroyed
history.scope_ja: Dushanbe and Varzob district
history.note_ja: About 400,000 people in the capital without clean water after storm damage; 26 km of road destroyed in Varzob; EM-DAT 2004 floods: 400,000 affected, USD 12 M.
history.jp_ja: Dependence on the single Varzob water intake is a recurring continuity issue for Dushanbe offices.

history.name_ja: 2007 Rasht earthquake, M5.2-5.5: 19 villages, 1,216 houses damaged
history.scope_ja: Rasht district, DRS
history.note_ja: Three boys killed, more than 12,000 affected; damage 11.5 M somoni (USD 3.3 M, UNCT). Same day a mudflow killed 12 in Asht (Sughd).

history.name_ja: 2008 cold wave and energy crisis in Dushanbe (coldest winter in 44 years)
history.scope_ja: Nationwide; Dushanbe residential areas without power at night and without heating
history.note_ja: Below -20 C from mid-January; Nurek reservoir low; from 26 Jan 2008 power cut to shops and markets in the capital; 2,000,000 affected and USD 840 M damage (EM-DAT); UN flash appeal USD 25 M.
history.jp_ja: Winter power rationing is the main cold-season continuity risk: plan generators and fuel.

history.name_ja: May 2016 mudflows: Rudaki (1,200 households), Varzob mudslide cut downtown Dushanbe's water
history.scope_ja: Rudaki and Nurobod (DRS), Panjakent and Ayni (Sughd), Rasht
history.note_ja: Mudflows 9-12 May 2016 hit 1,200 households in Rudaki alone; a Varzob mudslide left downtown Dushanbe without water for a day; 6 dead nationally by 3 June (REACT).

history.name_ja: 2021 Rasht earthquake, Mw 5.7
history.scope_ja: Rasht district, 20 km SE of Rasht town
history.note_ja: USGS us6000etys (12 km deep); Wikipedia list: 5 dead, 30 injured, 20+ buildings destroyed (the list misprints the date as 2021-10-07).

history.name_ja: August 2023 torrential rains: mudflows and flash floods in Vahdat, Rudaki and Varzob
history.scope_ja: Vahdat (17 dead), Rudaki, Varzob (Ajuk gorge); damage also in Hisor, Rasht, Tojikobod
history.note_ja: Toll rose from 13 (28 Aug) to 21 (30 Aug, CoES); Dushanbe-Vahdat-Lakhsh highway damaged; houses, roads and the Ajuk gorge water supply destroyed.
history.jp_ja: Commuter districts were hit; the eastern highway was cut for days.

history.name_ja: 2025 Rasht earthquake, Mw 5.8 (USGS yellow alert): 67 homes destroyed in Rasht and Tojikobod
history.scope_ja: Rasht and Tojikobod districts, 160 km NE of Dushanbe; intensity 3 in the capital
history.note_ja: 1 child dead, 16 injured; 67 homes destroyed, 195 partially and 186 lightly damaged, 4,004 people affected (CoES/IFRC DREF MDRTJ036); damage 17.78 M somoni (USD 1.66 M). USGS us6000q5q8, 8 km deep; M4.5 follow-ups on 17 June and 12 July 2025 caused no reported damage.

flood.note_ja: Spring rain floods Mar-May on the Kofarnihon, Varzob and Surkhob; snowmelt peak Jun-Jul

urban_flood.note_ja: Spring thunderstorms and hail; late-August storms (2023)

landslide.note_ja: Avalanches Jan-Mar on the Anzob/Khorog roads; mudflows Apr-Jun; glacier-melt debris flows Jul-Aug

cold.note_ja: January cold spells to -20 C with power rationing (2008)

haze.note_ja: Afghan dust storms Jun-Oct; winter inversion smog

water.note_ja: Late-summer irrigation shortfall; winter hydropower rationing

regions.pop_src: Sughd Region 2,707,300 (2020, Wikipedia infobox; about 2.9 M by 2024 assuming the national growth rate); Khujand city 191,000 (2019) with an urban area of about 770,000 (Wikipedia). third_party.
regions.desc_ja: Sughd is the northern third of Tajikistan: the western Fergana Valley lowland on the Syr Darya around Khujand (300 m), Kayrakkum reservoir, Konibodom and Isfara, plus the Zeravshan (Zarafshon) valley towns of Panjakent and Ayni and the Turkestan range behind them. It is the country's second economic centre (textiles, food processing, the Tajik Sea/Kayrakkum dam, the Istaravshan-Khujand road corridor to Uzbekistan) and connects to Dushanbe through the Anzob tunnel and Shahriston pass. Hazards are earthquakes along the Fergana Valley thrusts (1985 Kayrakkum), mudflows and flash floods in the Zeravshan and Isfara/Asht side valleys, Syr Darya and reservoir-related floods, and summer heat to 45 C.

extreme_cold.note: Khujand January mean 0.9 C, record low -22.8 C; the Fergana lowland is milder than the Zeravshan valley and Shahriston pass, where snow closes roads; the 2008 energy crisis showed high systemic vulnerability.

regions.hazard_scope_ja: ThinkHazard admin-1 level (2849 Sogd); Khujand district report 37606 (Hojenskiy) noted in hz_note_ja
regions.hz_note_ja: ThinkHazard rates Sughd High for river flood, urban flood, earthquake, landslide and wildfire and Medium for extreme heat and water scarcity; the Khujand district report (37606) is milder (river flood Medium, urban flood Medium, landslide Medium, earthquake High), because the city sits on the Syr Darya terrace while the High ratings come from the mountain districts (Ayni, Kuhistoni Mastchoh, Panjakent, Shahriston, Asht, Isfara) where loess and moraine slopes feed mudflow corridors into every village (Ayni July 2026: 672 households; Panjakent July 2021: 10-12 dead). Earthquake High reflects the active thrust belt of the western Fergana Valley (1985 Kayrakkum Mw 5.8, MMI IX, 29 dead; 1923 M6.5 south of Istaravshan) and GEM's 0.1-0.2 g 475-year PGA class, with Kayrakkum dam safety as the cascading concern. Water scarcity Medium: the region depends on Syr Darya releases from Kyrgyzstan's Toktogul and on the Zeravshan. Extreme cold is our own assumption (Khujand record -22.8 C; mountain roads closed by snow).

flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: WRI Aqueduct national riverine urban-damage curve for Tajikistan (100-yr USD 138.6 M, 1000-yr 202.2 M, 2010 baseline) with an assumed Sughd share of 25%. Reference events: July 1999 Asht/Ayni floods (18 dead, 50 missing, 167 houses destroyed in Asht), May 2008 Sughd rains (damage 63 M somoni), 9 May 2016 Panjakent mudflows (4 dead), 11 July 2026 Ayni (Darg/Kazdon) flash floods (672 households, 67 houses damaged).

scen.10: Spring (Apr-Jun) flash floods in the Zeravshan, Isfara and Asht side valleys: village roads, irrigation canals and a few dozen houses damaged
scen.50: 1999/2026-type: a cloudburst flood destroys 100-200 houses and bridges in Asht or Ayni, Khujand-Dushanbe road cut at Ayni/Anzob for days
scen.100: Syr Darya high water with Kayrakkum releases flooding low-lying parts of Khujand, Ghafurov and Konibodom plus valley-wide mudflows in Panjakent/Ayni
scen.500: Combined Syr Darya flood and failure of irrigation dams (Sardoba 2020-type event on the Uzbek side of the valley): tens of thousands evacuated, weeks of disruption to the rail and road corridor
scen.1000: Kayrakkum dam incident (reservoir 523 km2, embankments damaged in the 1985 earthquake) inundating the Syr Darya valley downstream (assumption; no published study used)

flood.method_ja: loss_max = 25% (assumed regional share) of the Aqueduct national 1000-year riverine urban damage (USD 202.2 M); k[RP] = Aqueduct national curve divided by its 1000-year value (derived). Depth, area and population scale with k (k^2.5 for population and downtime in the app); not a hydraulic model.
assumptions_ja: 25% share is an assumption: Sughd has about a quarter of the population and the Syr Darya lowland, but less floodplain than Khatlon (assumed 40%)
pop_max 0.05 = Aqueduct 1000-yr affected population (571,600) x 25% / 2.7 M
Aqueduct is riverine only and does not model the mudflows that cause most local damage (see the landslide row) nor dam failure
Sardoba (Uzbekistan, 2020) is cited as the 500-yr analogue although it lies outside the region

urban_flood.anchor_ja: Anchor: spring thunderstorms and hail flood Khujand, Istaravshan and Isfara streets for hours; Khujand is dry (173 mm/yr) so drainage is minimal. No loss statistics exist; all values are assumptions.

scen.10: Annual: hours of street ponding in Khujand and Ghafurov, market stalls and basements wet
scen.50: Half-day flooding of the city centre with hail damage to roofs and cars
scen.100: Multi-day storm with mudflows from the Mogoltau hills into northern Khujand suburbs
scen.500: Several days of flooding plus water and power loss
scen.1000: Drainage and water-system failure for a week

urban_flood.method_ja: Loss assumed from disruption days (about USD 5 M per day for the Khujand agglomeration) rather than statistics.
assumptions_ja: Sughd generates roughly a quarter of national GDP (assumption)
Depth and area refer to the Khujand-Ghafurov built-up area

quake.anchor_ja: Anchor: GEM national building-loss curve for Tajikistan (10-yr USD 29.1 M, 50-yr 268.7 M, 100-yr 478.1 M, 500-yr about 1.4 B, 1000-yr about 2.5 B) multiplied by 0.12, Sughd's share of national average annual loss in GEM's loss-by-region chart (USD 3.0 of 25.27 M). Reference events: 1985 Kayrakkum Mw 5.8 (17 km from Khujand, MMI IX, 29 dead, USD 200 M), 1923 M6.5 south of Istaravshan (87 km), 2011 Fergana Valley M6.2 (Batken, 14 dead in KGZ/UZB), 2023 Kuhistoni Mastchoh Mw 5.8 (318 houses damaged), 1946 Chatkal M7.5 about 150 km NE.

scen.10: M4.5-5.5 in the Kurama or Turkestan ranges felt at intensity 3-5 in Khujand (USGS: 31 M5+ within 150 km since 1950, 9 since 2000); no damage
scen.50: 1985 Kayrakkum-type M5.8 within 20-50 km: brick multi-storey blocks and factories in Kayrakkum/Ghafurov heavily damaged, dozens dead, reservoir embankments cracked
scen.100: 1923-type M6.5 in the Turkestan range or a 2011-type M6.2 in the eastern valley: damage in Istaravshan, Isfara, Konibodom; thousands homeless
scen.500: M7 on the North Fergana or Kurama thrusts within 60 km: widespread collapse of adobe and old brick housing across the lowland, Kayrakkum dam emergency, weeks without utilities
scen.1000: M7.5 (1946 Chatkal class) close to Khujand with liquefaction on the Syr Darya terraces and a Kayrakkum dam failure cascade (assumption)

quake.method_ja: Loss = GEM national loss curve x region share 0.12 (derived from GEM's regional AAL split). k only scales affected population and downtime (k^2.5 in the app). GEM counts buildings only; dams, canals and lifelines are excluded.
assumptions_ja: Share 0.12 follows GEM's AAL split; the 1985 event (USD 200 M in 1985 dollars from a single M5.8) suggests single-event shares in the Khujand area can be higher
pop_max 0.25 from the 1985 experience (8,000 homeless in a 30,000-person town) applied to a near-field M7+ on today's population
k values are judgement-based ratios for population and downtime, not from GEM

landslide.anchor_ja: Anchor: mudflows and debris flows in the Zeravshan valley (Ayni, Panjakent, Kuhistoni Mastchoh), Shahriston and the Asht/Isfara foothills. References: July 1999 Asht (18 dead), 22 July 2007 Asht/Oshoba resort mudflow (12 dead), May 2009 Ayni mudflow, 9 May 2016 Panjakent (4 dead), June 2017 Amondara/Panjakent (16 households) and Ayni (1 dead), 19 July 2021 Panjakent Dashti Kozi/Kishtudak (10-12 dead), June 2024 Shahriston/Kuhistoni Mastchoh mudflows, 11 July 2026 Ayni (672 households). Loss values are assumptions.

scen.10: Normal season: several mudflows in Ayni, Panjakent, Shahriston and Isfara; a few houses and road sections lost, 0-3 deaths
scen.50: 2021/2026-type: a night-time debris flow buries part of a village, 10+ deaths, 500+ households affected, Dushanbe-Khujand road cut at Ayni
scen.100: 1999-type valley-wide event across Asht and Ayni: hundreds of houses, bridges and canals destroyed, weeks of road closure
scen.500: Earthquake-triggered rockslides and loess flows in the Zeravshan gorge damming the river (Sarez-type mechanism at small scale)
scen.1000: Multi-valley cascade after an M7+ in the Turkestan range with landslide dams and outburst floods reaching Panjakent

landslide.method_ja: Loss, area and population are expert assumptions scaled by k; k[1000]=1 corresponds to a regional quake-landslide cascade.
assumptions_ja: loss_max USD 25 M at k=1 is an order-of-magnitude assumption
pop_max 0.02 (about 55,000 people) assumes dozens of Zeravshan and Asht valley villages affected
Rockfalls on the Anzob/Ayni road (e.g., 4 killed in May 2018) are included as mass movement

heat.anchor_ja: Anchor: Khujand record 45.9 C (July), July mean maximum 35.7 C; Tajikhydromet warned of +44 C for the Sughd plains in July 2018 and +47 C regionally in July 2025 with dust storms. Heat stresses cotton irrigation, the Syr Darya water balance and electricity imports.

scen.10: A week above 40 C: outdoor work limited, irrigation rationing in Konibodom/Isfara
scen.50: Two weeks of 42-45 C with power cuts and heat casualties among farm workers
scen.100: Record 46-47 C spell with glacier-melt floods in the Zeravshan
scen.500: Three-week heat dome with regional grid and water failure
scen.1000: Season-long extreme heat and crop failure across the Fergana lowland

heat.method_ja: Assumed losses from productivity, agriculture and power stress; no official heat statistics found.
assumptions_ja: pop_max 0.3 = residents exposed outdoors or without cooling at k=1
loss_max USD 15 M is an assumption
